introduction: On this Sunday, Sirach tells us that the prayer of the humble pierces the clouds. In the Gospel, a Pharisee and a tax collector go up to the temple to pray; the Pharisee boasts of his virtue, while the tax collector beats his breast and says, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Paul, near the end of his life, says, I have kept the faith. Let us come before God with humble hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is near to the brokenhearted. With humble hearts, let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may always be humble before God and merciful toward sinners. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor, the oppressed, orphans and widows: that God may hear their prayer. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who look down on others: that they may discover their own need for God's mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are near the end of their lives: that they may finish the race and keep the faith. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may pray with the humility of the tax collector. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God of mercy, you hear the prayer of the humble and lift up the lowly. Have mercy on us sinners, and make our prayer pleasing to you. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Be merciful to me, a sinner
reflection.body:
Sirach describes the God who hears the poor: "He will listen to the prayer of him who is wronged. He will in no way despise the supplication of the fatherless or the widow." And he says something beautiful: "The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds."

In the Gospel, Jesus tells a parable "to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others." Two men go up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stands and prays "by himself." His prayer is really about himself: "God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men... or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get." He does good things, but he uses them to look down on others.

The tax collector stands at a distance. He will not even lift his eyes to heaven. He beats his breast and prays seven words: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" Jesus says, "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." And he gives the reason: "for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted."

The tax collector's prayer has become one of the great prayers of the Church. It is the prayer of anyone who knows that we stand before God not because of our merits but because of his mercy.

Paul, in prison and near death, can say, "I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith." But he does not boast. He knows who gave him strength: "But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me."

This week, notice when you compare yourself with others to feel better. Instead, pray the tax collector's prayer often, and let it make you humble and merciful.
